title: Request for Comments Reference Guide
summary: A historical account that categorizes and summarizes RFCs 1 through 999, issued between 1969 and 1987. It cross-references them to show which are current, obsolete or revised. It replaces RFC 999.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1000 is a guide to the first 999 RFCs, published from 1969 through March 1987. It explains how the RFC series began, groups documents by topic, and gives a short description of each entry.

subtitle: A 1987 guide to RFCs 1 through 999, with categories, summaries, and cross-references.

tldr.problem: By 1987, the RFC series contained hundreds of documents, and readers needed a way to find them and see which had been revised or replaced.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1000 gives an account of the RFC series, sorts RFCs into topic categories, and lists the numbered documents with authors, dates, titles, and short descriptions.
tldr.outcome: It covers RFCs 1 through 999 from April 1969 through March 1987 and obsoletes RFC 999 and earlier indexes.

today: RFC 1000 is a historical guide published in August 1987, and the unit metadata lists its status as Unknown. It obsoletes RFC 999 and describes RFCs issued only through March 1987.

sections.title: What the Reference Guide Covers
sections.content:
RFC 1000 is a historical guide and topic index for RFCs 1 through 999, issued between April 1969 and March 1987. It cross-references documents to indicate which were current, obsolete, or revised in that period.

The RFC has three main parts: Stephen D. Crocker's account of the origin of the RFC series, a list of RFC numbers by topic, and a descending list of RFC entries with short descriptions. It obsoletes earlier indexes, including RFC 999.
sections.plainLanguage: This document helps readers find early RFCs and understand what each one covered. Its cross-references describe the status relationships recorded in the guide's 1987 snapshot.

sections.title: How the RFC Series Began
sections.content:
Crocker's account describes the early ARPANET project and meetings among the participating research sites. The group began writing down its discussions because protocol design questions needed to be shared between meetings.

Crocker chose the name Request for Comments to emphasize that anyone could contribute and that the notes were not official orders. The first notes addressed network and host software, while later work grew into a larger series of technical documents.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC series began as notes that people could use to share ideas and invite discussion. The name signaled that the documents were not official orders.

sections.title: Finding RFCs by Topic
sections.content:
The guide groups RFCs into broad categories and then divides some categories into topics. For example, file-transfer documents appear under Applications and File Transfer. RFCs about the Internet Protocol, ICMP, UDP, and TCP appear in different parts of the guide's hierarchy.

An RFC may appear in more than one topic listing. The category list is an index for the period covered by this guide, not a specification of how current documents are organized.
sections.plainLanguage: The topic index lets readers search by subject instead of number. Some documents appear in more than one category when they relate to multiple topics.

sections.title: The Numbered List and Summaries
sections.content:
The final part lists RFCs in descending number order. Each entry provides the RFC number, author, date, title, and a short description. Entries also note relationships to other documents, such as a later RFC obsoleting an earlier one.

The list includes entries marked Never Issued and lettered entries such as 017a. Its descriptions are brief guides to the documents, not replacements for reading the RFCs themselves.
sections.plainLanguage: The main list gives basic details and a short description for each RFC. It also notes when an entry was never issued or when another document replaced it.
